newsitem.title: GERMANY: RTL head calls for reform in German private TV.
newsitem.headline: RTL head calls for reform in German private TV.

text.p: German television draws huge advertising revenues but suffers from over-regulation, threatening the future survival of some private channels, the head of Germany's largest private station said on Wednesday.

The General Manager of the RTL network, Helmut Thoma, told a conference of advertising-driven industries in Hamburg that German commercial television desperately needed more flexible advertising rules for networks to be profitable.
Thoma called on advertisers, agencies and media companies to press for standards like those in the publishing industry, which allowed advertisers to place spots where they wished.

Under German media law, public broadcasters are not allowed to show advertising on television after 8 p.m. and commercial broadcasters must limit the number of times they interrupt programming for advertisements.
He also cited the rule that commercial breaks must contain a minimum of two advertisements as particularly harmful, considering the wide array of programmes available for viewers to surf to.
Thoma said German commercial television was hamstrung by a saturated market and the lack of cable fee income enjoyed by most national networks in the United States.
The intense competition in the German private television market, in which up to 19 stations are available in some areas, Thoma said, could force some stations out of the market.

Since the first German commercial stations were launched in 1984, only RTL and ProSieben have reached profitability. "This is not a healthy situation in the advertising-financed TV market," Thoma said.
Thoma praised the U.S. television market for ability support a variety of programming similar to Germany's while not squeezing networks out of the market.

"In the U.S., most stations live from some sort of fees or payments from cable companies," Thoma said. "In Germany we do not have this, which leads to the interesting situation that only two of the private networks are making a profit."
Thoma said the investment of telecommunications group Deutsche Telekom AG in buying and selling television programming might offer some cost outlay relief for networks.
